question:
Patient note:
A 66-year-old woman arrives in the pre-operative holding area this morning for an elective three-port laparoscopic cholecystectomy to address recurrent biliary colic and a 7-mm non-obstructing stone seen on recent ultrasound; the surgical team anticipates about 60 minutes of insufflation time and an overnight observation period. She stepped briskly from the visitor elevator, wheeled her own small suitcase, and required no assistance climbing onto the stretcher, noting that she still completes her neighborhood’s half-mile loop with her terrier twice daily and grocery-shops without a cart for support, so baseline ambulation is intact. Today’s operation is her first trip to the operating theatre in several years, and she confirms no procedures, endoscopies, or hospital admissions for anything surgical during the past month. Review of the prior month is otherwise notable for an episode of substernal pressure while gardening twelve days ago; emergency evaluation revealed elevated troponin I peaking at 2.3 ng mL⁻¹ and dynamic T-wave inversion in the anterior leads. Coronary angiography that same day showed a discrete 70 % lesion in the proximal left anterior descending artery that was treated with a drug-eluting stent, after which her chest discomfort resolved; ventricular function remained preserved at 55 % ejection fraction, and she completed a short cardiac-rehabilitation orientation last week without exertional symptoms. She has had no orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle swelling, or weight gain, and takes guideline-directed medical therapy consisting of aspirin 81 mg, ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, high-intensity atorvastatin, and low-dose metoprolol. Her medical history also includes a stage III sigmoid adenocarcinoma resected three years ago followed by twelve cycles of FOLFOX; a low-profile subcutaneous chest port was placed before chemotherapy and remains flushable with good blood return, though it has not been accessed since her last surveillance colonoscopy six months ago showed no recurrence. She has no personal history of inflammatory bowel disease such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease. She denies cough, sputum production, or chronic bronchitis and has never used inhaled therapies. She has not had any episodes of pneumonia, bronchitis requiring antibiotics, or other acute pulmonary infections in the past month. No physician has ever diagnosed heart-failure exacerbations, clotting events in the legs or lungs, cerebrovascular accidents, long-bone fractures, pelvic injuries, spinal cord pathology, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, or systemic infection that required intensive care. She has not worn casts, braces, or splints and has maintained full mobility since completing chemotherapy. Family members have no history of venous thrombo-embolism or known heritable thrombophilias. She never smoked, enjoys a glass of red wine with dinner on weekends, and denies hormone replacement, corticosteroid bursts, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or selective oestrogen-receptor modulators. Vital signs obtained 20 minutes ago show temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 132/76 mm Hg, pulse 68 beats min⁻¹ and regular, respirations 16 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air; body mass index is 27 kg m⁻². She appears comfortable, converses in full sentences, and is oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Airway examination reveals Mallampati class II view, three-finger thyromental distance, normal neck extension, and intact dentition. Carotid upstrokes are brisk; jugular venous contour is not elevated; the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced; and S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear throughout with good excursion and no adventitious sounds. The abdomen is soft and nontender except for mild right upper-quadrant discomfort on deep palpation; surgical scars include a healed 10-cm left lower-quadrant laparotomy incision with no herniation. Extremities are warm and well perfused, calves measure 36 cm bilaterally, there is no pitting oedema, cord-like structures, or varicosities, and pedal pulses are 2 + and symmetric. Neurologic screen shows 5/5 strength in all major muscle groups and intact sensation to light touch. Skin inspection of the anterior chest reveals the outline of the implanted venous access device beneath an intact dressing; there is no erythema, fluctuation, or tenderness over the reservoir pocket, and catheter position was last confirmed by radiograph after stent placement. A single 20-gauge peripheral cannula in the left forearm is running lactated Ringer’s at a keep-open rate; no other peripheral or limb lines are present. Morning laboratory results demonstrate haemoglobin 13.6 g dL⁻¹, haematocrit 40 %, platelets 248 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 6.9 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 139 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.2 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.89 mg dL⁻¹, AST 21 U L⁻¹, ALT 23 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.6 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 12.1 s with international normalised ratio 1.1, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. A focused twelve-lead electrocardiogram printed on arrival shows normal sinus rhythm at 64 beats min⁻¹, a PQ interval of 160 ms, QRS 90 ms, and no acute ST-segment shift compared with the tracing from her catheterisation admission. Last evening’s upright posterior–anterior chest radiograph depicts clear lung fields, an intact diaphragmatic silhouette, and the port catheter tip projecting over the cavo-atrial junction. Sequential pneumatic calf sleeves lie at the foot of the stretcher ready for application after intubation, and, per institutional protocol for patients on dual antiplatelet therapy, no anticoagulant has yet been administered until surgical haemostasis is assured. She has been nil per os since midnight, last voided an hour ago, has removed her own dentures and jewellery, and verbalises understanding of the operative plan, expected recovery course, and the importance of early ambulation after transfer to the ward.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
Use the preoperative Caprini score, which adds points for patient and procedural risk factors for venous thromboembolism.
- Age 61–74 years: age 66 → 2.
- BMI >25 kg/m²: BMI 27 kg/m² → 1.
- Myocardial infarction within the past month: troponin-positive coronary event 12 days ago → 1.
- Planned laparoscopic surgery lasting >45 minutes: approximately 60 minutes → 2.
- Current or prior malignancy: previously treated sigmoid adenocarcinoma → 2.
- Central venous access: chest port remains in place with its catheter tip at the cavoatrial junction → 2. The peripheral IV adds nothing.
She is independently mobile and has no other documented qualifying risk factors. The planned procedure is counted once.
Sum: 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10.
Final answer: 10
